reason: Diazepam and its metabolite (half-life ~100 h) are still active 1–3 days after stopping, so the model still shows calm. Real long-term users already notice early rebound; the model's benzodiazepine tolerance is incomplete.
SSRI discontinuation syndrome (anxiety, dizziness, 'brain zaps') is not modelled; its mechanism is not well understood. In the model the slowly clearing drug is still calming on day 1.
MAO-inhibitor discontinuation (agitation, sometimes delirium) is not modelled; the model's MAO recovers smoothly.
The direction is right (less anxiety), but too weak: the long-term adaptations that make MAO inhibitors strong anti-anxiety drugs are only partly modelled.
The cocaine 'crash' (dysphoria as levels fall) is not modelled; it likely involves acute tolerance and dopamine-receptor adaptations within the hour that this model lacks.

The chronic context judges ~4 h after the morning dose, when a short-acting heroin dose has largely worn off. Breathing suppression in tolerant users at the time of a dose is covered by the rank tables.

Bupropion's antidepressant effect is not reproduced: its weak dopamine/noradrenaline reuptake block (~20% DAT occupancy) barely moves the model's slow plasticity variable, which mainly responds to serotonin, glutamate and psychedelics.
In the model caffeine's alerting effect grows as adenosine builds up during the day, so it lasts into the evening; felt alertness in studies fades after 3–6 h, although effects on sleep persist.
See caffeine arousal time course: rising adenosine during the day makes the model's caffeine effect last too long.
